e-8224.knowledge_point: Identifying Sets That Are Not Vector Spaces
e-8224.problem:
Let $V$ be the set of all real polynomials of degree exactly $3$, equipped with the usual addition and scalar multiplication operations. Complete the following sentence:

*$V$ is **not** a vector space because $\textrm{_________}\,.$*

- the sum of two polynomials of degree $3$ may not be a polynomial of degree $3$

- $V$ does not contain the polynomial $-p(x)$ for every $p(x) \in V$

- addition of polynomials is not commutative
e-8224.worked_solution:
The correct answer  is as follows:

*$V$ is **not** a vector space because **the sum of two polynomials of degree $3$ may not be a polynomial of degree $3$.** *

For instance, if $p(x) = 1 +x^3$ and $q(x) = 1-x^3$, then $p(x)$ and $q(x)$ are in $V.$ However  

$$
\begin{aligned}p(x)+q(x) & =(1+{x}^{3})+(1-{x}^{3}) \\  & =2\notin V.\end{aligned}
$$

On the other hand:

- Addition of polynomials is commutative.

- For any polynomial $p(x)$ of degree $3$, the corresponding negative polynomial $-p(x)$ also has degree $3.$

*Statement: *

*If $\mathbf{w}$ is a vector such that $\mathbf{w}+\mathbf{w} = \mathbf{w}$, then $\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{0}.$* 

*Proof:*

$$
\begin{aligned}w+w & =w &  & [\,\text{given}\,] \\ (w+w)+(-w) & =w+(-w) &  & [\,\text{add [math]-\mathbf{w}[/math] to both sides}\,] \\ w+(w+(-w)) & =w+(-w) &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ w+0 & =0 &  & [\,\text{axiom A4}\,] \\ w & =0 &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,]\end{aligned}
$$

The axioms:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{[A1]}:x+y=y+x & \text{[A5]}:1\cdot x=x \\ \text{[A2]}:(x+y)+z=x+(y+z) & \text{[A6]}:\alpha (\beta x)=(\alpha \beta )x \\ \text{[A3]}:x+0=x & \text{[A7]}:(\alpha +\beta )x=\alpha x+\beta x \\ \text{[A4]}:x+(-x)=0 & \text{[A8]}:\alpha (x+y)=\alpha x+\alpha y\end{aligned}
$$

Let I be the set of all functions f:R→R of the form f(x)=2ax, where a∈R. Complete the following sentence:

I is not a vector space (with respect to function addition and scalar multiplication of a function by a real number) because _________.

a
addition of functions is not associative
b
I does not contain the zero element
c
addition and scalar multiplication of functions do not satisfy the distributive laws
d
addition of functions is not commutative
e
1⋅f≠f for some f∈I
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The correct answer is as follows:

I is not a vector space (with respect to function addition and scalar multiplication of a function by a real number) because I does not contain the zero element.

Indeed, f(x)=2ax>0 for all x∈R for any a∈R, hence the zero function z(x)=0∉I.

On the other hand:

  • Addition of real valued functions is associative. ✓

  • 1⋅f=f for all f∈I. ✓

  • Addition and scalar multiplication of polynomials satisfy the distributive laws. ✓

  • Addition of real valued functions is commutative. ✓

From top to bottom, fill in the blanks and hence complete the proof of the following statement using the axioms $[\text{A}1]-[\text{A}8]$ given below.

*Statement:*

*Given any $x\in V$, if $y$ is a vector such that $x+y=0$, then $y=-x.$* 

*Proof:*

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =0 &  & [\,\text{given}\,] \\ (x+y)+(-x) & =0+(-x) &  & [\,\text{add }-x\text{ to both sides}\,] \\ (y+x)+(-x) & =(-x)+0 &  & [\,\text{axiom A1}\,] \\ (y+x)+(-x) & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ y+(x+(-x)) & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ y+0 & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom A4}\,] \\ y & =-x &  & [\,\text{axiom A3}\,]\end{aligned}
$$

The axioms:

$$

From top to bottom, fill in the blanks and hence complete the proof of the following statement using the axioms $[\text{A}1]-[\text{A}8]$ given below.

*Statement: *

*If $x$ is a vector such that $-x+w=w$ for some $w\in V$, then $x=0$* 

*Proof:*

$$
\begin{aligned}-x+w & =w &  & [\,\text{given}\,] \\ x+(-x+w) & =x+w &  & [\,\text{adding }x\text{ to both sides}\,] \\ (x+(-x))+w & =x+w &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,\,] \\ 0+w & =x+w &  & [\,\text{axiom A4}\,] \\ w & =x+w &  & [\,\text{axiom  A3}\,] \\ w+(-w) & =x+w+(-w) &  & [\,\text{adding }-w\text{ to both sides}\,] \\ w+(-w) & =x+(w+(-w)) &  & [\,\text{axioms  A2}\,] \\ 0 & =x+0 &  & [\,\text{axiom __}\,] \\ 0 & =x &  & [\,\text{axiom  A3}\,]\end{aligned}

$$

$$
